Gen Chem isn't memorization.
It's patterns. We'll find yours.

If you've felt "bad at chemistry" — you're not. Somewhere along the way, a foundation skill got skipped — a mole conversion, a Lewis structure rule, a pH shortcut — and everything after it felt harder than it should. Each skill teaches you the move, walks you through it, lets you practice, and only marks it "mastered" when you can do it cold three times in a row. LAB · 04

      
Lab toolkit — glassware, indicators, errors

      
The DAT GC reserves ~5% of questions for lab basics — which glass to use, which indicator catches which equivalence, where students systematically lose digits. Cards below are the canonical reference. Not glamorous; free points.

    

  


  

    
Glassware — accuracy hierarchy

    

      

        
VF

        
Volumetric flask

        
±0.05 mL · ~0.1%

        
Use: preparing a solution at a precise volume (e.g., dilute to 250.00 mL). Calibrated for ONE volume only — fill to the etched line.

        
Trap: measuring AT a volume other than the etched line.

      

      

        
VP

        
Volumetric pipette

        
±0.02 mL · ~0.1%

        
Use: transferring a precise fixed volume (10.00, 25.00 mL). Calibrated TD ("to deliver"). Touch tip to glass to release the meniscus.

        
Trap: blowing out the last drop — that volume is intentionally retained.

      

      

        
BUR

        
Buret

        
±0.05 mL · ~0.1%

        
Use: titrations — variable, precise dispensed volume. Read meniscus at eye level; subtract initial from final.

        
Trap: air bubble in the tip throws off the volume actually delivered.

      

      

        
GC

        
Graduated cylinder

        
±0.5 mL (50 mL) · ~1%

        
Use: approximate volumes where ±1% is fine (rinse water, solvent additions).

        
Trap: using for a quantitative dilution — use a volumetric flask instead.

      

      

        
FL

        
Erlenmeyer / beaker

        
±5% or worse

        
Use: reaction vessel, mixing, holding — NOT for measuring volume.

        
Trap: trusting the side markings as if they were calibrated.

      

      

        
BAL

        
Analytical balance

        
±0.0001 g · 4 decimal places

        
Use: precise mass for stoichiometry, standards. Tare with weighing paper or boat.

        
Trap: hot objects — convection currents bias the reading low.

      

    

  


  

    
Acid-base indicators — match pKa to equivalence pH

    

      

        
Indicator
pH range
Color (acid → base)
Best for

      

      

        
Methyl orange

        
3.1 – 4.4

        
red → yellow

        
WB + SA titration (eq pH < 7)

      

      

        
Bromocresol green

        
3.8 – 5.4

        
yellow → green

        
Acidic-range titrations (around pH 4–5)

      

      

        
Litmus

        
5.0 – 8.0

        
red → blue

        
Quick qualitative test (not titrations)

      

      

        
Bromothymol blue

        
6.0 – 7.6

        
yellow → blue

        
SA + SB titration (eq pH = 7)

      

      

        
Phenolphthalein

        
8.2 – 10.0

        
clear → pink

        
WA + SB titration (eq pH > 7); also works for SA+SB

      

    

    

      Rule: the indicator's pH-change range should bracket the equivalence pH. Phenolphthalein for acetic-acid + NaOH; methyl orange for ammonia + HCl; bromothymol blue (or phenolphthalein) for HCl + NaOH.
    

  


  

    
Common error sources — where students lose digits

    

      

        
Parallax

        
Reading the meniscus from above or below the line. Always at eye level — bottom of the meniscus for clear liquids, top for opaque (e.g., KMnO₄).

      

      

        
Air bubble in buret tip

        
The bubble's volume is read as titrant delivered, but it never reached the flask. Always purge before initial reading.

      

      

        
Wet glassware (the wrong kind)

        
Burets and pipettes can be wet with the titrant being measured (rinse with it). They should NOT be wet with water — that dilutes. Volumetric flasks SHOULD be wet with water (you're filling to the mark).

      

      

        
Indicator overshoot

        
Over-titrating past color change adds extra moles of titrant. Add dropwise near the endpoint and use a contrasting white background.

      

      

        
Hot weighing

        
A hot crucible reads low on the balance (rising convection lifts it). Cool to room temp in a desiccator before final mass.

      

      

        
Non-quantitative transfer

        
Leaving residue in the original beaker. Rinse 2-3× with the solvent and add to the receiving flask. Critical for quantitative analysis.

Solubility rules — predict precipitation

      
Compounds that follow these rules are soluble. The exceptions are insoluble.

      

        
SOLUBLE
Group 1 + NH₄⁺
All salts of Na⁺, K⁺, Li⁺, NH₄⁺ → always dissolve

        
SOLUBLE
NO₃⁻, ClO₃⁻, ClO₄⁻, C₂H₃O₂⁻
All nitrates, chlorates, perchlorates, acetates → always dissolve

        
USUALLY SOLUBLE
Halides (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻)
Except with Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺ (insoluble)

        
USUALLY SOLUBLE
Sulfates (SO₄²⁻)
Except Ba²⁺, Pb²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ca²⁺ (low) — "BPS = no SO₄"

        
INSOLUBLE
Carbonates (CO₃²⁻), Phosphates (PO₄³⁻), Sulfides (S²⁻)
Except group 1 + NH₄⁺

        
INSOLUBLE
Hydroxides (OH⁻)
Except group 1, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺ (Ca²⁺ borderline)

      

      

        Memorize: "NAG SAG" mnemonic — Nitrates, Acetates, Group 1, Sulfates (mostly), Ammonium, Group 17 (mostly) = soluble.

Higher E° = stronger oxidizer (wants electrons more). The cathode in any cell has higher E° than the anode.

Activity series of metals — for single-replacement

      
A metal HIGHER on this list will replace any metal BELOW it from a compound. Memorize roughly: Li > K > Ba > Ca > Na > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au.

      

        
1Li, K, Ba, Ca, NaReact with cold water

        
2Mg, AlReact with steam

        
3Zn, Fe, PbReact with acids (replace H)

        
—HReference — metals above replace H from acids

        
4Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, PtDon't react with most acids · "noble metals"

      

      
Lock: A metal above another in this list will displace it. Zn(s) + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu(s) (occurs) · Cu(s) + ZnSO₄ → no reaction (Cu is below Zn).

    


    
    

      
Reaction types — pattern recognition

      

        
Synthesis (Combination)
A + B → AB
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O · Two reactants combine

        
Decomposition
AB → A + B
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ · One reactant breaks apart (often heated)

        
Single-Replacement
A + BC → AC + B
Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu · Driven by activity series

        
Double-Replacement
AB + CD → AD + CB
AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃ · Driven by precipitate / gas / water

        
Combustion
CₓHᵧ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
Hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + water (always exothermic)

        
Acid-Base (Neutralization)
acid + base → salt + H₂O
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O · Special double-replacement

        
Redox
e⁻ transfer (oxidation states change)
Always changes oxidation states · LEO (lose=ox), GER (gain=red)

      

      
Driving forces for double-replacement: precipitate forms (use solubility rules), gas evolves, OR a weak electrolyte forms (water, weak acid). If none, no reaction.

START · 01

      
Diagnostic — find your floor

      
Twenty questions, fifteen minutes. Not graded. We're mapping where you're solid and where there's a gap. The result is a skill heatmap and a path. That's it.

    

  


  

    

      

        
D

        

          
Before we start: three things to know

          
This isn't a test. Read each note before you click begin.

        

      

      

        

          
You can't fail this

          
We're not testing you to grade you — we're trying to find where you got stuck, so we can teach you that exact thing. The more honest you are about what you don't know, the more useful this is.

        

        

          
Take your time

          
No timer. If you nail a question, the next one gets a little harder. If you miss, the next gets easier. That's how we figure out exactly where you are.

        

        

          
Rate your confidence

PERFORMANCE · 04

      
Pacing ladder

      
Time pressure unlocks only after untimed mastery. Each tier requires 80% accuracy at the previous tier. We never put a stopwatch in front of you on day one.

    

  

  

    

      
PACE

      
Four tiers · climb when ready

      
No timer until you're ready for one. Then we ratchet down: 90s → 60s → DAT-pace.

    

    

    

  







  

    

      
PERFORMANCE · 02

PERFORMANCE · 05

      
Test-day simulation

      
40 questions. DAT pace. No breaks. Per-topic accuracy and a missed-question walkthrough at the end. Don't take this until your pacing ladder is at 60s/Q across most patterns — otherwise it'll just rattle you.

PERFORMANCE · 04

      
Daily 5-minute drill

      
Spaced repetition (SM-2) schedules problems based on your performance: missed = next day, easy = exponentially longer. Drills pull from your due-for-review queue first, then refresh recently-attempted problems, then layer in new ones from skills you've started. Difficulty ramps up across the drill (level 1 to level 3).
